html:
The Itelmen are a native people of the Kamchatka Peninsula in the Russian Far East. The map shows them from 1530 to 1700. Their language belongs to the Chukotko Kamchatkan family, distantly related to those of the Koryaks and Chukchi, and is now almost extinct.

They lived mainly by catching salmon in the rivers, hunting seals and gathering plants and berries. They wintered in houses dug partly into the ground and used dog sleds.

The Cossack Vladimir Atlasov led a Russian force into Kamchatka in 1697, part of the Russian conquest of Siberia. Russians demanded tribute in furs and put down Itelmen revolts in the early 1700s. Scientists of the Great Northern Expedition in the 1730s and 1740s described their way of life in detail. Smallpox in the late 1760s killed many. Over time they mixed with Russian settlers, and their descendants were often called Kamchadals.
